name: Plan and schedule field work
summary: Work planners turn released capital, maintenance and customer work orders into weekly and daily crew schedules for line, cable and station crews. For each order they check that the design is complete, material is in stock, permits and the customer's site are ready, locates are requested and switching is booked, then fit it into crew capacity and confirm readiness just before the work. The process is slow because orders wait for material, customers and crew capacity, and unstable because trouble calls, storms, absences and weather pull crews away. Jobs that are not ready when the crew arrives waste crew time and send the order back into planning.

baseline.org_archetype: A municipally owned Ontario distributor with about 350,000 customers and roughly 60 line, cable and station crews planned by a central work planning group.
baseline.notes: Unit of work is one work order taken from release to completion; a large capital order may cover several crew days but is scheduled as one order.

trigger: A capital, maintenance, service or connection work order is released for scheduling in the ERP.
end_state: The order has been worked by a crew, recorded complete and closed for scheduling.

volume.seasonality: Construction peaks from May to November; frost and snow in January to March slow underground and civil work, and the spring locate backlog delays digging jobs.

evidence.note: Organisation file estimate kept: about 60 crews each finishing several orders a week, plus inspection and joint-use orders.

surge.cause: major storm pulls crews to restoration and forces the planned schedule to be rebuilt

evidence.note: Author's estimate; the organisation file assumes one to four declared major events a year. During a storm planned work stops and every scheduled order is rescheduled, so planner workload multiplies.

Twelve planners; about 50 minutes of planner time per order including rescheduling at 2,000 orders a month needs about 13 FTE, so the planning group is fully loaded and batches routine maintenance orders.
Weekly approval and daily rebalancing.
Weekly assignment review for overhead jobs.
Weekly assignment review for underground jobs.
Corrects about 7% of packages returned from planning.

systems.name: ERP: general ledger, work orders, purchasing, inventory, fixed assets
Mobile workforce management and field tablets
Document management and engineering drawing repository
Geographic information system (asset and network model)
Ontario One Call member portal and locate management

steps.name: Release work order to planning queue
steps.description: When design, approvals and funding are complete the originating group sets the work order to released in the ERP, which places it in the planners' queue with its estimate, crew type, required date and linked design package.
outputs: released work order in planning queue

evidence.note: Standard ERP work order status flow.

steps.name: Review work order package
steps.description: A work planner opens the released order, the design drawings in the document store and the material list, checks that scope, crew type, estimated hours and required date make sense, and assigns a priority. Orders with missing drawings or unclear scope go back to design.

error.defect_description: Crew type or hours estimate wrong, found when the crew arrives.

evidence.note: Author's estimate; incomplete packages are a common cause of planning rework.

steps.name: Correct the design package
steps.description: A design technologist reopens the job, adds the missing drawing, corrects the material list or clarifies the scope with the planner, and re-releases the order.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Check material availability
steps.description: The planner checks the order's material reservation in the ERP against stock on hand, sees whether poles, transformers, switchgear or cable are in the warehouse, and asks stores or a buyer to expedite anything short.

evidence.note: Share short of material is the author's estimate; transformer and switchgear lead times lengthened in 2021-2022.

steps.name: Wait for long-lead material
steps.description: The job is held until the supplier delivers the missing transformer, switchgear, cable or poles to the warehouse; the planner sees the receipt in the ERP.

evidence.note: Author's estimate of supplier lead times, longer in 2021-2022 supply-chain disruption.

steps.name: Check permits and site readiness
steps.description: The planner checks that the municipal consent or road occupancy permit is in hand, that the customer or developer has finished civil work and has electrical inspection where needed, and that easements and access are settled.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Chase customer, developer or city
steps.description: The planner calls or emails the developer, customer's electrician or the city to find out when the site, inspection or permit will be ready, notes the expected date and parks the order until then.

evidence.note: Author's estimate; customer and developer delays are a leading cause of unready work.

steps.name: Book date with customer
steps.description: For service and connection jobs the planner calls the customer or contractor to agree a date when the site will be accessible and anyone needed will be present, and records the commitment on the order.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Request locates and flag switching needs
steps.description: For jobs that dig, the planner submits a locate request through the One Call portal with the dig area and start date; for jobs on energized plant, the planner flags the need for work protection so the crew supervisor applies for a switching order.

error.defect_description: Locate area too small or start date wrong, so the locate does not cover the dig.

control.basis: Ontario Underground Infrastructure Notification System Act, 2012: request locates before excavating

evidence.note: Locate requests are due at least five business days before digging; share of orders that dig and timing are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Build draft weekly crew schedule
steps.description: Each week the planner fits ready orders into the next week's crew calendar in the scheduling spreadsheet or ERP scheduling board, balancing crew hours, due dates, customer commitments and the order of jobs on the same feeder. Orders that do not fit wait for a later week.

evidence.note: Backlog waiting for crew capacity is the author's estimate; Bain describes the trade-off between loose schedules (idle crews) and tight ones (missed commitments).

steps.name: Lines supervisor reviews assignments
steps.description: At the weekly planning meeting the overhead lines supervisor checks which crew gets each overhead job, matches skills and equipment to the work, and moves jobs that need a larger crew or a digger derrick.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Underground supervisor reviews assignments
steps.description: At the same meeting the underground supervisor checks the cable crew assignments, confirms civil contractor dates for duct and vault work and adjusts the order of splices.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Approve and publish weekly schedule
steps.description: The work planning and dispatch supervisor resolves conflicts between groups, approves the week's schedule and publishes it to crews, stores (for material picking) and the control room (for switching).

control.basis: Supervisor approval of the weekly crew schedule

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Confirm job readiness two days ahead
steps.description: Two working days before the job the planner checks that locates are complete in the One Call portal, the switching order is approved, material is staged, the permit is valid and the customer is still ready. Jobs that are not ready are rescheduled before the crew is sent.

evidence.note: Not-ready share is the author's estimate; jobs not ready when the crew arrives are the main cause of lost crew time.

steps.name: Chase outstanding locates or switching
steps.description: The planner calls the locate dispatcher or contractor and the switching planner to find out whether the outstanding locate or switching order will be done in time, and asks for priority if the crew date is fixed.

evidence.note: Late locates were common across Ontario in this period; chase times are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Reschedule job
steps.description: The planner removes the job from the crew's week, records the reason (locate, material, customer, weather, crew pulled to trouble), fills the slot with another ready job if one exists, and puts the order back into the weekly planning pool.

evidence.note: Bain recommends tracking cancelled and last-minute jobs as schedule stability; times are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Build daily schedule and issue job packets
steps.description: The day before, the planner turns the week's plan into each crew's day in the mobile workforce system, attaches drawings, locate numbers, switching order number and customer notes, and prints packets for crews that still use paper.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Rebalance crews at start of day
steps.description: At the start of the shift the dispatch supervisor adjusts the day for absences, crews held over on trouble or storm work, and broken-down trucks, moving or dropping jobs. Forecast high wind, lightning or freezing rain puts overhead jobs on hold.

evidence.note: Shares are the author's estimates; trouble and storm work take priority over planned work.

steps.name: Hold job for weather
steps.description: The supervisor keeps the job on the crew's list but holds it until the weather clears, assigning the crew yard or underground work in the meantime, and releases it again when conditions allow.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

steps.name: Record crew completion status
steps.description: After the crew works the job the planner reads the completion status in the mobile workforce system (complete, partly complete, not done and why), updates hours in the ERP and puts unfinished work back into planning.

next.condition: partly done or found not ready on site

evidence.note: Bain found crew wrench time of about 40% at a large utility, much of the loss from poor planning; shares here are the author's estimates.

steps.name: Close scheduling record and report compliance
steps.description: Weekly, the planner confirms completed orders are closed for scheduling, and the team reports schedule compliance (jobs done as planned against jobs scheduled) and reasons for misses to operations management.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

exceptions.name: Long-lead material
exceptions.description: A transformer, switchgear or cable is not in stock and the job waits weeks for delivery.

exceptions.name: Customer or permit not ready
exceptions.description: The developer's civil work, electrical inspection or the city permit is not in place; the planner chases and parks the order.

exceptions.name: Not ready two days out
exceptions.description: Locates, switching or material are missing at the readiness check and the job is rescheduled to a later week.

exceptions.name: Crew pulled on the day
exceptions.description: Trouble, storm work or absences take the crew and the job is bumped.

exceptions.name: Found not ready on site
exceptions.description: The crew arrives and cannot finish because of site, material or scope problems; the remaining work goes back into planning.

benchmarks.unit: calendar days from release to completed
benchmarks.population: Released distribution work orders at a mid-size Ontario distributor, 2019-2022

evidence.note: Author's estimate: maintenance orders are usually worked within two to four weeks of release, capital jobs wait longer for material, permits and customers. No published distribution figure was found.

benchmarks.unit: share of crew time on hands-on work
benchmarks.population: One large US utility before a productivity programme

evidence.note: Single-utility diagnostic; shows the scale of time lost to travel, waiting and unready jobs.

pain_points.description: Jobs found not ready at the two-day check, on the morning of the job or on arrival send orders back to weekly planning and leave crews idle or on filler work.

evidence.note: Bain reports idle crews and wrench time near 40% from poor planning at US utilities.

pain_points.description: Locate and switching readiness are tracked in separate systems (One Call portal, OMS) and checked by hand.

evidence.note: Author's estimate from the systems in use.

pain_points.description: Long-lead material and customer site delays hold capital orders for weeks.

evidence.note: Author's estimate.

sources.title: Locates - safe digging (information for contractors)
sources.supports: Locate requests go through Ontario One Call at least five business days before digging (ten for multi-address requests); colour-coded ground markings; stay 1.5 m from marked cables and hand dig or hydrovac near them; request a re-locate when marks are unclear or expire; near high-voltage cables Hydro Ottawa places a 'Do Not Proceed' sticker or notice, the excavator completes a Request to Excavate form, and Hydro Ottawa replies within 48 business hours.

sources.title: Industry group praises crucial reforms to Ontario's utility locates system
sources.supports: Locates are legally due within five business days but 'as high as 85 per cent' of requests are late; Ontario One Call data showed 49 per cent of tickets took longer than 15 days; idle time costs about $1,000 an hour in sewer and watermain work; Bill 93 reforms (shared locates, 60-day minimum validity, dedicated locators).

sources.title: Field service: Reenergizing a hidden asset
sources.supports: At one US utility less than 50 percent of field time was spent on actual maintenance or construction work; one utility scheduled so loosely that crews were idle 50 to 60 percent of the time while another scheduled so tightly it missed customer and compliance dates; recommends tracking the share of jobs cancelled and schedule stability.

sources.title: Boosting a utility's workforce productivity (case study)
sources.supports: Undated case study (the programme began in 2010); year is the access year. Field diagnostic at a large US utility found crew wrench time of about 40 percent; poor planning caused idle time and schedule gaps; productivity rose by 25 percent or more in the first year after the change.

assumptions: Loaded costs are taken from the organisation file (wage times 1.40 for benefits, pension, payroll taxes and overhead).
The weekly planning meeting is shown as one review step per order for the relevant supervisor; minutes are the supervisor's share of the meeting for that order.
The wait before the weekly schedule step stands for backlog waiting for crew capacity; it is the largest single source of elapsed time.
Crew work itself is outside this process (it belongs to construction and maintenance processes); its duration is entered as the wait before completion status is recorded.
design-technologist is not listed among this process's roles in the organisation file; it is included because returned packages are corrected by design.
Rescheduled orders loop back to weekly planning; about one order in four is rescheduled at least once, which matches the instability the organisation file describes.
